title: "The Three-Tree Model"

# The Three-Tree Model

After this page you can name Git’s three snapshots of the same project and say which command copies between them.

## Three snapshots, one project

Everyday Git is three versions of the same tree:

| Name | On disk | Role |
|------|---------|------|
| Working directory | your files | What you edit |
| Index (staging area) | `.git/index` | What the *next* commit will contain |
| HEAD commit | an object in `.git/objects` | Last committed snapshot on this branch |

```text
working directory  --git add-->  index  --git commit-->  HEAD
                 <--git restore--      <--git restore --staged / git reset--

 ~/desk/desk-api/              .git/index                 .git/objects
 README.md, src/…              next commit                last commit (HEAD)
```

- `git add` copies working-tree bytes into the index (and writes **blob** objects).
- `git commit` writes a **tree** from the index, then a **commit** pointing at that tree and at the current HEAD, then slides the branch name forward.
- `git restore <file>` copies from the index (or a commit) onto the working tree.
- `git restore --staged <file>` copies from HEAD into the index, leaving your working-tree edit in place.

There is no fourth “GitHub tree.” A remote is another repository’s names plus objects you have fetched.

## Why the index exists

The index lets the next commit be a chosen subset of what is on disk. You can edit five files and commit two.

```bash
echo "ok" >> README.md
echo "wip" >> notes.txt
git add README.md
git status
# README.md is staged; notes.txt is not
```

`git commit -a` copies **already tracked** files from the working tree into the index and commits. New files still need `git add`. Prefer explicit `git add` until that distinction is boring.

## `status` is the three-tree report

```bash
git status
```

Git compares:

- working tree vs index → “Changes not staged for commit”
- index vs HEAD → “Changes to be committed”
- untracked files → paths the index does not know

When all three match, `status` is clean. That is the happy state after a commit.

## `reset` in one sentence

`git reset` moves HEAD and optionally the index and working tree. Soft / mixed / hard are which of the three trees follow. Chapter 7 (reset) and chapter 17 (reflog) use this on purpose. For now, prefer `git restore` to throw away an unstaged edit, and `git restore --staged` to unstage.

## Check it

```bash
git status
git diff              # working tree vs index
git diff --staged     # index vs HEAD
```

If `git diff` is empty and `git diff --staged` is not, the next commit already contains the change. If both are empty and `status` still lists a file, it is untracked — `git add` it.
